Title: Mesoscale Processes Driving Offshore MCS Initiation in the South Asian Summer Monsoon: Insights from an Ensemble-Based Satellite Data Assimilation Experiment
Brief Abstract: Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) are the primary rainfall contributors over the Bay of Bengal (BoB) during the South Asian summer monsoon. Previous studies have established a strong connection between MCS initiation over the BoB and diurnal gravity waves propagating from India. However, the precise role these waves play in triggering offshore MCSs remains unquantified. In this study, we analyze a typical MCS event, representative of the climatological spatiotemporal characteristics of MCS initiation in the region, to investigate the relative roles of diurnal gravity waves and other mesoscale processes in offshore MCS initiation. An ensemble-based satellite data assimilation (DA) experiment is conducted, assimilating all-sky infrared radiances from Meteosat-8 into the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model. The ensemble forecast, initialized from DA analyses, shows that many ensemble members accurately capture both the timing and location of MCS initiation. The analysis of the "successful" members reveals diurnal gravity waves play a significant role in enhancing lower-tropospheric moisture and destabilizing the offshore environment. Surprisingly, similar gravity waves and destabilization are also present in members that failed to capture MCS initiation. Further analysis indicates that land-breeze front from northern Sri Lanka is a key factor distinguishing successful from "unsuccessful" members, which, in successful members, is strong enough to lift air above the level of free convection (LFC) and lead to MCS initiation. Accurately simulating the land-breeze front depends on the correct representation of pre-MCS clouds and surface winds. This suggests that while diurnal gravity waves contribute to environmental destabilization, surface and boundary layer processes are crucial for the practical predictability of offshore MCS initiation.

Title: Evaluating Planetary Boundary Layer and Land Surface Models via Dual-Polarization WSR-88D and Flux Tower Observations
Brief Abstract: Recent work has taken advantage of the existing national network of dual-polarization WSR-88D radars to produce accurate daytime planetary boundary layer (PBL) depth estimates for every radar volume scan (roughly every 10 min or less) at WSR-88D sites across the United States. We expand on this work by comparing hourly forecasts of daytime PBL depth from the Mellor-Yamada-Nakanishi-Niino eddy diffusivity-mass flux (MYNN-EDMF) PBL scheme to estimates obtained from WSR-88D observations for calendar year 2022. Forecasts from the operational Rapid Refresh (RAP) model that uses the Advanced Research version of the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF-ARW) Model are used to generate this large dataset for analysis. We find that MYNN-EDMF forecasts of PBL depth can differ significantly from WSR-88D observations in both timing of growth and maximum depth of the PBL with consistent biases in PBL depth across regions and seasons. These biases are then evaluated through the comparison of parameterized surface sensible and latent heat fluxes to those observed by flux towers located near selected radar sites. We find that errors in predicted PBL depths are strongly correlated with the over-/underestimation of surface sensible heat flux. Further assessment of modeled soil moisture reveals that the land surface model utilized by RAP is likely contributing to PBL depth biases in summer months through erroneous drying of soil, which increases surface sensible heat flux and therefore PBL depth.

Title: Synoptic and Mesoscale Variability in Convective Boundary Layer Depth Observations from Dual-Polarization WSR-88D Radars
Brief Abstract: The convective boundary layer (CBL) is one of the most important and variable layers in the atmosphere, yet observations of the CBL have been limited. Recent results show that the dual-polarization WSR-88D radars can observe CBL depth using differential reflectivity observations on most days with observations available every 10 min or less. We apply a CBL depth tracking method to observations from 48 WSR-88D dual polarization radars spread across CONUS for 2014 and 2022. Results indicate that mean monthly CBL depth over CONUS is smallest in December at 632 m and largest in June at 1606 m. Objective analyses of daily maximum CBL depths show large horizontal variability with synoptic and mesoscale processes contributing to this variability. CBL depths are deeper in the warm sector of midlatitude cyclones compared to surrounding regions, with some days showing anomalies in maximum daily CBL depth of over 1000 m in the warm sector. Mesoscale processes such as lake and sea breezes and precipitation also influence CBL depths. The time of maximum CBL depth shifts throughout the year, being earliest in the winter months and over an hour later in the summer months with regional variations. CBL depth increases most rapidly 1-3 h prior to local noon, with decreases in CBL depth starting 3 h after local noon. Calculating CBL depth routinely from the WSR-88D network will be valuable for air quality and aviation forecasts, model verification, and data assimilation.

Title: Transatlantic Data Science Academy Website
Brief Abstract: The Transatlantic Data Science Academy (TDSA) was launched in 2023 by the UK Met Office and NOAA to develop data skills for weather and climate science. It focuses on attracting and growing a skilled workforce in data science, data engineering, research software engineering, and data assimilation through training, exchanges, joint projects, and hackathons. It addresses extreme weather impacts from climate change and includes activities like establishing a Data Assimilation Consortium, staff exchanges (e.g., Kate Huxtable and Tom Hill at JCSDA), attendance at AMS2024, and plans for 2024-25 including placements, learning frameworks, a sandpit with hackathons, and communication efforts.

Title: Common Community Physics Package: Fostering Collaborative Development in Physical Parameterizations and Suites
Brief Abstract: The Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) is a state-of-the-art infrastructure designed to facilitate community-wide development of atmospheric physics parameterizations, support their interoperability among different modeling centers, and enable the transition of research to operations in NWP and climate modeling. The CCPP consists of two elements: the Physics (a repository of parameterizations) and the Framework (an infrastructure for interfacing the parameterizations with host models). The CCPP is a community resource: Its latest release has 23 primary parameterizations, which can be organized into six supported suites. It is distributed with a single-column model to facilitate physics development and experimentation. The Developmental Testbed Center provides support to users and developers. A key aspect of the CCPP is its interoperability, that is, its ability to be used by multiple host models. This enables synergistic collaboration among groups dispersed over various institutions and working on various models. In this article, we provide an overview of the CCPP and how it is being used in two leading modeling systems. The CCPP is part of the Unified Forecast System (UFS), is included in the NOAA operational Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS) version 1, and is slated for use in all upcoming NOAA global and limited-area UFS applications for operations. Similarly, the CCPP has been integrated into the Navy Environmental Prediction System Using a Nonhydrostatic Engine (NEPTUNE) model and is undergoing testing for the upcoming transition to operations. These experiences make physics interoperability a reality and open the doors for much broader collaborative efforts on ESM development.

Title: Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) Physics - UFS Fork
Brief Abstract: The Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) is a collection of atmospheric physical parameterizations (physics schemes) and a framework for integrating them into various atmospheric models. This specific repository is the UFS community's fork, containing the physics suites used in NOAA's Unified Forecast System. It is designed to facilitate the rapid transition of physics innovations from research to operations. The package is compliant with the CCPP Standard Names dictionary and supports both global and regional applications, including the UFS Weather Model and the Single Column Model (SCM).

Title: Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) Framework
Brief Abstract: The CCPP Framework is the specialized infrastructure that connects the CCPP physics schemes with a host model (such as the UFS Weather Model). It serves as the architectural "glue" that allows physics suites to be swapped or updated without modifying the underlying model core. The framework includes tools like ccpp_capgen to automatically generate the necessary code for data exchange between the model and physics schemes based on metadata. By providing a standardized interface, it enables a "plug-and-play" environment for atmospheric physics, supporting both operational forecasting and modular research development.

Title: Nested-EAGLE
Brief Abstract: Nested-EAGLE is a development repository for a data-driven atmospheric forecast model. It features a high-resolution nesting over the Continental United States (CONUS) within a coarser global model framework. The project focuses on leveraging machine learning and data-driven techniques to enhance regional forecasting accuracy while maintaining global consistency. The repository includes multiple configurations (e.g., 0.25deg-06km and 1.00deg-15km), observation processing tools, and an ERA5-based prototype.

Title: eagle-tools
Brief Abstract: eagle-tools is a Python-based software package designed for processing, evaluating, and visualizing anemoi-based EAGLE Machine Learning (ML) models. The toolkit provides a suite of command-line utilities to perform large-scale inference over multiple initial conditions, calculate averaged error metrics (RMSE and MAE), generate spatial error distributions, and compute power spectra. Additionally, it includes capabilities for visualizing predictions against targets through both static figures and movies. It is primarily used for research and development on high-resolution, data-driven forecast models.

Title: Community Global Workflow (GW)
Brief Abstract: The Global Workflow framework is a unified, highly configurable end-to-end infrastructure designed to orchestrate, execute, and verify complete global numerical weather prediction cycles for the Unified Forecast System Weather Model (UFS-WM). The framework seamlessly integrates separate modeling and infrastructure submodules-including atmospheric pre-processing, data assimilation (via the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation [GSI] and the JEDI-based Global Data Assimilation System [GDAS] Application), core forecast execution, post-processing, and verification (using the METplus-based EMC_verif-global package). Built to streamline both operational tasks and collaborative public research, it supports multiple configuration tiers across various NOAA High-Performance Computing (HPC) platforms and native cloud platforms like Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure.

The framework seamlessly integrates separate modeling and infrastructure submodules-including atmospheric pre-processing, data assimilation (via the Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation [GSI] and the JEDI-based Global Data Assimilation System [GDAS] Application), core forecast execution, post-processing, and verification (using the METplus-based EMC_verif-global package). Built to streamline both operational tasks and collaborative public research, it supports multiple configuration tiers across various NOAA High-Performance Computing (HPC) platforms and native cloud platforms like Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure.
